newsitem.title: FRANCE: Britain deserted CJD sufferers - victim's mother.
newsitem.headline: Britain deserted CJD sufferers - victim's mother.

text.p: A mother whose son died of Creutzfeld-Jakob Disease said on Thursday that the British government had deserted victims and their families.
"The relatives feel we've got no one on our side," Briton Dot Churchill, whose son Stephen died 18 months ago from the new strain of CJD, told Reuters.
She said the families of the CJD victims had demanded an independent inquiry into the British government's handling of mad cow disease, but that British ministers had refused.

The British government had also rejected the relatives' request for special funding to help nurse people diagnosed as having CJD, a slowly incubated brain-wasting disease believed to result from eating infected beef.

The relatives were now considering whether to take legal action against the Ministry of Agriculture, said Churchill, who since her son's death has thrown herself herself into the fight to help others suffering from CJD.
"The government thinks it will just go away," she sighed.

British epidemiologists said on Wednesday the medical time bomb planted by mad cow disease could kill tens of thousands of people. The best to hope for, they said, would be a total of no more than 75 victims. The worst might be as many as 80,000.
"The government is responsible. They took the risks in the 1980s so they should do what they did with AIDS and pick up the tab," Churchill continued.
She said she could not believe ministers and Conservative Euro-MPs who said the government bore no responsibility for the BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) epidemic.
"It's come from Britain, we know it was in the feedstuff, it's in the British herd," she pointed out. "If we take Britain out of it, who's responsible? The decisions must have been taken somewhere."
Churchill said letters from the families to the leaders of Britain's political parties and European Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler had received a deeply unsatisfactory response.

Prime Minister John Major's office had replied there was no need for special hospital provisions for CJD and said an inquiry was unnecessary since there was already an independent advisory committee on BSE-CJD.
"The committee looks ahead at plans and research but it doesn't look back. They obviously don't want to find out what went wrong," Churchill concluded.
She said Liberal leader Paddy Ashdown had told the families he supported an independent inquiry but did not appear to have done anything to take the campaign forward.
Labour party leader Tony Blair and Commissioner Fischler had not even acknowledged their letters.

Contacts with other European Commissioners had proved more positive, said the diminutive Churchill, who runs a bed and breakfast establishment in south west England and says she finds meetings with top European officials a draining experience.
Consumer Commissioner Emma Bonino and Padraig Flynn, the commissioner responsible for public health and safety, had both agreed a single top official should be put on in charge of BSE and CJD.
"At the moment, no one is responsible for this. It falls between the three commissioners, Flynn, Bonino and Fischler," Churchill said.

Flynn had also told her on Thursday he would consider financing translations for other parts of Europe of a newsletter produced by the British CJD support network giving updates on the disease and help for victims and their relatives.
"I can't bring my son back but we want to make it easier for the families who'll have to deal with (CJD) in future," said Churchill, whose home phone doubles as the CJD helpline.
Twelve people have so far died from CJD in Britain. Three more cases have been diagnosed, one of them in France.

Churchill and other victims' relatives plan to return to the European Parliament with CJD specialists on February 19, the day Euro-MPs are due to examine a report criticising both the British government and the European Commission for their handling of the BSE-CJD crisis.
The report, drafted after a four-month investigation by a special cross-party committee of inquiry in the European Parliament, is good but incomplete in Churchill's view.

None of the families had been called to give evidence and British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg's refusal to appear before the committee of inquiry meant the Euro-MPs had not been able fully to examine the crisis, she said.
On the basis of the report, Euro-MPs may next month recommend legal action against the British government.
Hundreds of thousands of British cattle had BSE at the height of the epidemic, which started in 1986. Small outbreaks took place in a few other countries.
